title: The junior's bill
spec: U09 · isolation, and the tokens it honestly costs
intro: Isolation is the most expensive arm on the whole grid — more expensive than sending everything. Read the receipt that proves it, understand exactly where the tokens went, and learn the task shape where the price inverts.
foot: Do it for real: ask Q9 in isolated and read the receipt's tool line.

steps.title: Send the junior to the archives
narrative: Isolate is the fourth strategy: give a sub-agent its own clean window, let it do the messy work, and hand only the conclusion back to the parent. The exploration — forty records read, three dead ends, two re-reads — never crosses the threshold into the parent's context.

MedFlow's isolated mode implements the honest version. A second model call receives a minimal clean context for the data-gathering subtask, and its bounded summary — not its working — feeds the answering call. Crucially, the sub-call's tokens are billed to the parent's tool layer, so the price is on the receipt rather than hidden in another window.
steps.youDo: Switch the mode toggle to isolated and ask Q9: "Summarize member M-2001's authorization history."

terminal.text: Summarize member M-2001's authorization history: how many requests and what were the outcomes?
assemble(mode=isolated) → spawn sub-agent, charter: "M-2001 authorization history"
sub-agent: clean window, reads requests, returns memo → billed to tool layer

steps.title: The receipt nobody wants to publish
narrative: The answer is correct. The bill is 1,796 input tokens — against notes at 167 and naive at 1,700 for the same question. Isolation did not save anything here; it cost slightly more than sending the entire domain dump.

Note the second line of the bill too: the output is 52 tokens against every other arm's 26. Two completions were generated — the sub-agent's memo and the parent's answer — and both are billed. Isolation buys two clean windows and pays for two calls.

steps.title: Where the tokens actually went
narrative: Read the layer breakdown across all ten isolated cells and the mechanism is unmistakable: retrieved is 0 on every single row, and the tool layer carries 1,696–1,757 tokens. The parent window really is clean — it never sees a domain dump. The sub-agent's window is where the mess went, and that window is billed to the tool layer.

So the honest sentence is not "isolation is expensive". It is: isolation moves the cost from the parent's retrieved layer into the parent's tool layer, and on a single-shot question it adds a second call's worth on top. Across the whole grid, isolated totals 18,040 input tokens against naive's 16,948 — 6.4% more than the control arm that sends everything.
steps.claudeSays: Nothing went wrong. The sub-agent explored, summarised, and handed back; the parent answered from the memo. The receipt simply refuses to pretend the sub-call was free.

before.title: MEASURED — retrieved 0, tool ~1,700, on all ten

steps.title: The course ships the loss instead of hiding it
narrative: Isolated's median is 1,805 tokens against naive's 1,696, at identical 10/10 correctness for the arms that pass. That number could have been buried — fold the sub-call into another window, report only the parent's input, and isolation would look like a 96-token miracle.

It stays on the board for the same reason compressed's Q9 failure stays on the board. A benchmark that only shows wins is marketing. And the loss carries information: it tells you the exact task shape isolation is worst at, which is the shape this grid measures — one question, one answer, nothing reused.

steps.title: Where the price inverts
narrative: Invert the task shape and the arithmetic flips. The sub-agent's exploration never enters the parent window, so it never compounds: on turn twelve the parent is still carrying a memo, while a naive session is re-carrying every dump it ever pulled plus twelve turns of history (U08's climbing curve).

Three conditions make isolation pay: the exploration is much bigger than the conclusion; the conclusion will be referenced again; and the exploration would otherwise pollute the parent's attention budget for the rest of the session. Parallelism is the fourth — three sub-agents reading three members concurrently return three memos, and the parent pays three memos rather than three transcripts, forever after.

Be precise about what the grid does and does not prove here. The shipped isolated mode re-runs the sub-agent on every question, so this grid never measures amortisation at all — it measures the worst case ten times. The break-even curve below is illustrative; computing it on your own session is the U09 lab.

steps.title: The hand-back contract is the technique
narrative: None of that arithmetic exists without a bounded hand-back. A sub-agent that returns its whole exploration has re-imported the mess isolation was hired to contain — that is naive mode with an extra call and an extra bill.

So the contract is enforced, not hoped for: a bounded charter in, a bounded memo out, asserted before the memo is allowed into the parent. Break the assertion in the lab by returning the transcript instead of the memo, and watch the hand-back get refused.
steps.youDo: In the U09 lab, return the full transcript from the sub-agent and confirm the budget assertion refuses it.

lines: transcript = explore(charter, records)   # 40 reads, dead ends, re-reads
return transcript                        # the archive room follows you home

after.title: AFTER — a memo, and only a memo
